text:
Short answer: no, don't lead with that — and be careful about it, because in your situation it's the weakest thing you have, and raising it could cost you credibility on the points that are actually strong.

**Why the all-male panel doesn't help your case**

A discrimination claim needs you to have been disadvantaged *because of* a protected characteristic. You're a man. The person appointed is a man. Four men chose between two men and picked the other one. There's no coherent story in which your gender worked against you here. If you argue that an all-male panel favoured a man, the obvious reply is: so did you benefit from that, and the comparison between you two had nothing to do with sex.

Where an all-male panel genuinely matters is (a) as background in a claim brought by a woman who was passed over, or (b) as a governance and compliance problem for the employer in its own right. Many public systems require gender balance on appointment committees for public bodies — if that applies where you are, the panel's composition may well be a procedural defect the school board or an equality ombudsman would care about. But that's a complaint about *them*, not a route to compensation or reconsideration for *you*. If you fold it into your own case, a decision-maker will read it as scattershot, and it invites them to dismiss the whole letter as a disappointed candidate throwing everything at the wall.

**What's actually strong**

Two things, and they're both much better than the panel's gender.

1. **The qualification comparison.** On the announcement's own description, you have a master's degree in educational leadership and five years actually doing the deputy's job. He has "taken courses in school leadership" and ten years of teaching. Note what's missing from his description: any leadership *experience* and any leadership *qualification* beyond coursework. Ten years of teaching is relevant but it's not the same category as five years of school management. In most public-sector appointment frameworks the authority must appoint the most qualified applicant and must be able to show, on the record, how it compared them. The phrasing of that announcement is a gift to you — it reads as though whoever wrote it couldn't point to leadership credentials, so they described training instead.

2. **The unanswered request.** In most public administration systems a rejected applicant has a right to written reasons, and the authority has a duty to respond within a reasonable time — often a defined one. Two weeks of silence may already be a breach, and regardless it's a concrete, documentable failure that you don't have to argue about. It also helps you procedurally: you generally can't challenge reasoning you haven't been given, so their silence is holding up your ability to assess the decision.

**What I'd do**

Send a second written request, dated, referencing the first. Ask specifically for: the reasons for the decision, the comparative assessment of the shortlisted candidates against the stated criteria, the criteria and any scoring used, and the minutes of the panel's deliberations. Ask for your own interview notes if they exist. Set a deadline and say that if you don't receive a response you'll take the matter to the school board or the relevant ombudsman. Keep the tone procedural, not aggrieved.

Separately, the more promising question than gender is **whether the appointee was already known to the panel** — an internal candidate, a colleague, someone with a prior relationship to a panel member. Favouring the familiar is a far more common reason a less-qualified candidate wins, and unlike your gender theory, it has a real chance of being true and of mattering. Worth quietly finding out.

One caveat: your rights here depend heavily on jurisdiction — whether this is a public or private school, what the applicable administrative and equality law says, and what deadlines apply for challenging an appointment. Those deadlines can be short. If you're seriously considering a challenge, get a short consultation with a lawyer or your teachers' union now rather than after you've exhausted the correspondence; the union in particular will have handled this exact scenario before.
